utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And could we please have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Mark Harmon and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Daniela Tasic, Tina Drolec, Eric Tully, Chad Mair, Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Do we have a witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Hopefully we have a witness today, Your Honour. I'm not in charge of bringing him over here from the -- his accommodations. I assume he is in the witness waiting-room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Could we call him in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We hope you're well rested. Just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration that you took at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We left each other last night having a brief conversation with regard to the Mujahedin. And I'd like to spend a few more moments talking about some of the contextual issues that involving around the time of July 1995. You had mentioned in your testimony that, I believe, that there was also apart from the presence of Mujahedin within the Muslim Bosnian army, there was also smuggling occurring that went through Tuzla. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the smuggling was the continuing effort to move man power and supplies into particularly the eastern enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa in order to keep the 28th Infantry Division supplied. I don't know how that has to deal with the Mujahedin, in so much as I'm not aware of any of them in those eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to the issue of smuggling, were you aware of a meeting that occurred in 1994 in Tuzla with various members of the United States air force and Bosnian Muslim army members concerning supplying ammunition and other necessary equipment to the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In the research that you did, did you come across any discussions about a secret airport or air strip was being built in a place called Visiko?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then we won't talk about it. In terms of -- I'm moving to your report now in a general sense. Would it be fair to say that in your view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have which report we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Oh, reports, I'm sorry. I thought I heard the singular.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you did, I dropped the S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that when you were engaged in your analysis as you were writing your various reports that you attempted to be as objective as you possibly could be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as technically accurate as you could be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I think, as a matter of fact, an expression of your concern about accuracy was evidenced at the beginning of your testimony here where you corrected I believe on two occasions some errors that you saw in your report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's been a component of most of the trials there have been minor errors that have been identified that we've corrected over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. And obviously whenever you come across -- whenever you come across an error whether it be by review of your report or through the process of examination or cross-examination, that's something that you have remedied at a later point in time, if a later point in time came about; correct? It's an evolutionary process.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remedied in the sense of my discussion and testimony. I have not updated the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But as you did here, actually it was in Courtroom II, but as you did here when you came across an error, you at least alerted the Prosecution with regard to that error?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before the formation of the VRS, there was -- and I'm going to -- I believe for you familiar territory, the JNA, as a military organisation that embodied the entirety of the SFRY, the former Republic of Yugoslavia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the JNA, you had occasion to review a number of documents in that regard in your analysis of the structure of the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically we had access to documents from the former JNA 4th Corps and 17th Corps, which I did use as a model to determine whether or not the VRS had organised along the same lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the issue of whether or not the VRS had organised along the same lines, you studied, I take it, the former situation that existed in the SFRY prior to its breakup; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the historical context of the SFRY for the most part. My interest was in the military doctrine and an organisation and processes of the former Yugoslav national army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you use the term "military doctrine," I take it you're talking about a principle that dictates military behaviour in the most general of senses.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- in the term of doctrine, yes, it is the most general of senses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could you explain for the Chamber, if you could, what the term "military doctrine" embodies.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term embodies the general principles by which a military force exists within a nation state. The doctrine of a particular military force within a country, in turn, drives many of the other factors that are necessary for a military to survive, such as a doctrine will drive what type of equipment that that military will purchase over time. It will drive the types of units that they want, how they want to organise them, and how they want to man them. It will drive their entire professional training and educational process. It drives their budget. So within the former SFRY, for example, their doctrine was one known as All People's Defence. And within that doctrine, that is how they organised their armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say within their doctrine, that is how they organised their armed forces, you've mentioned All People's Defence. And I take it at that point what you're talking about is what occurred in the former Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply put, All People's Defence was a doctrine, a defence doctrine that was driven by many of the lessens of World War II, where the Yugoslav national leadership recognised that, particularly between the former Warsaw Pact block and the NATO block in Europe that they would be able to conventionally defend Yugoslavia from a threat. So going back to the lessens of World War II and their occupation by the Nazis, their defence doctrine took the view that they would have a nucleus of a professional army and some conventional forces, but that in large part all military-aged men would be capable of engaging in military activities in a partisan or guerilla warfare type of campaign, the goal being to make anyone's thought of occupying Yugoslavia so expensive in terms of time, manpower, and other resources that they would not do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the doctrine as it applied to the All People's Defence, you've mentioned partisan or guerilla warfare. Would it be fair to say that what you're talking about there is that the entire nation would be involved in mass resistance to an invader, either from the west or the east?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the notion of the All People's Defence, the All People's Defence necessarily included within it a decentralised form of operation; correct? One that would be able to be easily used in a guerilla warfare setting.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was envisioned over time that the more centralised conventional forces would fight the best that they could, and that in order to buy the time for Territorial Defence units and those guerilla forces to organise themselves while the actual military operations were viewed as being along a decentralised manner, by municipality in many respects they were still envisaged to be centrally organised by the top leadership of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to, once again, the Territorial Defence units would it be fair to say that they were -- I'm going to put this in these terms: That they were formed locally; they were under the direction of the opstina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not necessarily under the direction of the opstina, but the opstina or municipality would be responsible for raising the forces. They would be responsible for provisioning them to the best of their ability. It was envisioned that that civilian organisation, then structure, of the municipality would play a very large role in supporting the continued existence of those particular Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Those defence units were trained for combat operations close to home; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since those defence units were in effect made up of people who had served their conscripted time in the JNA, they had the same ability to do that. However, you know, it's not a question of training. They were organised for local operations, is probably the more accurate way of saying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. I'll accept that as a -- as a modification. And with regard to where they were organised, by that mean if they were organised in the lowlands or the mountains, the organisation was based upon the particular geographic area in which they were located, among other things; correct? Mountain fighting being different than lowland fighting.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, because I didn't study the entire former SFRY in that respect, whether that's accurate. What I can say is that most of those Territorial Defence units were organised as light infantry units which would make them capable of fighting in a variety of environments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Those individuals who were not fighting age, which I think was between of, let's say, 16 to 64. The rest of the population, what was their function, if you know, with regard to the All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what their specific functions would be, I mean, other than generally to support the war effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now apart from the Territorial Defence aspect of the military doctrine that you have been explaining to us in the former Yugoslavia, there was also a standing professional army; correct? The JNA, independent of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The JNA stood as a separate arm of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And they -- by that I mean the JNA, they standing as a separate part of the armed forces were professional army. True?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With rules and regulations that existed internally with regard to such issues as command and control; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And other organisational issues that were perhaps not necessarily germane to the Territorial Defence in the former Yugoslavia, right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on what issues you would be referring to. For example, the same military officers who had a command in the JNA could subsequently go over and, you know, have command issues or be part of the Territorial Defence, so issues of command and control and many of those particular regulations would be the same for both. So it would depend on which particular area that you wanted to discuss, whether or not the operating procedures of the JNA and the operating procedures of the Territorial Defence would differ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the former Yugoslavia, did you come to an understanding of how those two forces would operate together? Would one be subordinate to the other; would they work in tandem with each other?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In their particular doctrine, and in this case, what I refer to is the provisional corps regulations. I mean, it envisions that in a number of cases that the professional army and the Territorial Defence would work in tandem on the modern battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to them working in tandem in the modern battlefield as you've described it, this was, once again, a military doctrine that was essentially defensive in nature; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to one of the things you mentioned earlier in your testimony, which I believe was that the military doctrine embodies the national objectives of the state, with regard to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, first of all, can you tell us when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was formed as a nation state?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you offhand which date after World War II that would have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; I'm talking about the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume at this juncture we're talking sometime after April of 1992, after Bosnia had gained their -- or had basically voted for independence. I couldn't tell you when the exact date would be on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the Republika Srpska, can you give us a date for that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- what would become the Republika Srpska, first, was known as the -- was it autonomous Serb republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I believe, started to surface in documents as at least a governmental body as early as January of 1992. It later officially was redesignated the Republika Srpska approximately November of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the formation of the Republika Srpska Krajina, did you in your analysis do any study of the Republic of Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Neither factual nor historical, in terms of an understanding of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just broadly within in the terms that it existed, there was a conflict related to that. But given that my focus was primarily on Eastern Bosnia, it was just outside the scope of study for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the formation of the army, the VRS in the Republika Srpska, could you tell us when the army was formed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was -- I guess their official birthday is June of 1992 is when they called themselves when they were formed. The reality was that it was a much more fluid process. For example, General Mladic was appointed the commander of the army in early April 1992, and at that point, from April, May, through June, most of his efforts were in fact working to try and create the army. From an amalgamation of locally raised units and former JNA units that in some form or another were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. With regard to what you've just said, that his efforts were in fact working to try and create the army, in your research an analysis, did you make a determination of how many actual JNA soldiers remained at the Republika Srpska? I'm sorry, that assumes something that that we haven't discussed yet, which is there come a time when the JNA left the region; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the JNA withdrew through the month of late April and early May 1992. I they were out by either the 16th or the 17th officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And where did they go, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the JNA formations that withdrew went to either Serbia or Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the JNA formations that withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina, some of the JNA formations had previously been on a journey, having previously withdrawn from the area of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now with regard to those that remained in the Republika Srpska? Did you have an idea of how many actual individuals or soldiers remained?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that figure off the top of my head. I know that in the VRS's an annual report for 1992 that they actually do provide those figures of the professional soldiers an officers of the JNA who were serving with the VRS. So I know that the answer is there; I just don't know the figure off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to General Mladic's effort to create an army, you mentioned that this was an amalgamation of various forces, to use the -- I think a relatively liberal term for the moment. And those force would have been those remaining soldiers, correct, and the Territorial Defence? Would be the two main components of that amalgamated army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In some areas, for example, in the Krajina, where you had large bodies of the former JNA that did remain, they organised as the 1st Krajina Corps and had you some professional units or the nucleus of some professional units as well as a lot of the Territorial Defence units that had been stood up by the municipalities that were ultimately absorbed in the 1st Krajina Corps. In Eastern Bosnia, for example, where none of the former JNA formations that were there remained, that corps was formed by a variety of locally raised Territorial Defence units exclusively. And I guess the last element that was integrated in the army over time was some of these rogue paramilitary organisations that were running around the Krajina and eastern Bosnia that were either disbanded or absorbed into the regular army by the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 6073 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to some of the efforts that were occurring in terms of the amalgamation issue that you have discussed, I'd like to you take a look at this particular document and see whether this comports with what you were saying. And I'm looking at the language at paragraph 1, the decision.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It reflects the initial routes as out of those local or regionally based TO units and defence staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is this one of the documents that you were analysing when you were involved in your research with regard to the general issue concerning the structure of the army and the evolution of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could go down to the bottom. Just scroll down to the bottom. If we could have this admitted as defendant' next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It appears to not be complete on the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page. Sorry, I apologise, yes. All right. As a matter of fact, thank you so much, Mr. Harmon. You reminded me of something that I had forgotten for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the explanation, it indicates in paragraph 1 that the TO staffs shall remain in their existing formation and composition and they shall be established TO staffs in newly established Serbian municipalities along the same lines. And I take what that means there, and you clearly understand this from all of the research you've done, is that the TOs are going to remain under the control of the opstinas. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially at this point in time it was a very decentralised command and control model, and the local TOs engaged in military operations or other activities strictly at the direction of their local Crisis Staff or other municipal leaders. There wasn't the overall national level, to use that word, command and control apparatus in place. So most of that was at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have this marked -- admitted as defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we now have P190 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if you would take a look at Article number 2, understanding that this -- this document deals with decisions made on the 12th of May, does this reflect, in your opinion, the beginning of the evolution of the Territorial Defence from being only under the control of the opstinas to being integrated into the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the appointment - I again, think I said April, so I'm corrected if it's 12 May - the appointment of General Mladic as the commander of the Main Staff of the army and the organisation of that Main Staff subsequently is the efforts to take these Territorial Defence organisations and start to meld them into a national type of army and one that could start dealing with conflict-related issues on a national level rather than at each individual municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at that point in time, and if you could be of some help to me here, it seems to me that you have a bit of a dilemma, and the dilemma being as follows, which is that you have a professional army that has a military doctrine that envisions some of the aspects of the Territorial Defence notion, and you have a Territorial Defence component that is strictly defensive in nature in a civil war. So it would seem to be somewhat of a dilemma in term of how best to proceed forward. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's an accurate characterization of the issue. I think the problem that they were facing was that the -- there was no national military hierarchy to look at the strategic big picture of the military. And the problem that they were facing is that the municipal Crisis Staffs were very often focussed on the immediate threat in their particular municipality. So you this had odd situation where military forces in one municipality wouldn't be performing any duties, because they had already accomplished the missions that they wanted to do and didn't see it as their role to go and assist in another municipality. So there was no large coordinated strategy to deal with these issues. They were all being done piecemeal. And I think that was the doctrinal problem that the Republika Srpska leadership had, is that while they had national objectives with the six strategic goals, for example, they couldn't realize those as long as they were continuing to operate on a very decentralised manner at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the difficulty that existed, as a matter of fact, as between the military doctrine at hand and the entire manner in which the Territorial Defence had been set up is something that had been previously recognised at the time of the JNA was involved in fighting; correct? And if I might be of some assistance to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 6292 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It might be the easiest way to get you to -- what I'm trying to suggest to you. It's going to be page 5 in the B/C/S, which we're ultimately going get to. And as soon as the -- is that the English? There we go. Okay. First of all, just if we could take a look at the dates just so you know what the date is, which is 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 6 of the document in English and page 5 in B/C/S. And I'm specifically going to paragraph number 4. And if we could have that blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from the discussion about the JNA not wishing to be involved in this particular war, as we get to paragraph 4, it says: "This war is specific in many aspects. "Exactly. The JNA was not prepared for this kind of war. Many tradition ideas and values that we used to build our defence system upon have been of no use to us at all. We had to approach an all-out transformation of the army and of the doctrine of its use." So this is clearly a dilemma that was faced by the JNA. And I take it this is the same dilemma that was faced by General Mladic when he was attempting to build his army, after May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the first component of the JNA, I agree. I mean, the reality is that I'm not aware that any major army, for that matter, has a doctrine or practices portraying to the level of what happens when the country falls apart in civil war. It is just not something envisioned obviously and the JNA found itself right in the middle of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, General Mladic, he had already been working through that process, and his goal was basically taking the existing pieces that he either had in Bosnia or that were left behind by the JNA and taking them from a largely decentralised force and creating an overarching command and control element that would allow them to focus the existing force towards more operational and strategic goals, as opposed to just being involved in municipal-level activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And, once again, in terms of talking about military doctrine, would it be fair to say that at the higher levels it's really quite conceptual, in terms of what military doctrine is, and as you go down to the lower levels, then really what you're dealing with is operational issues and tactical issues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And in fact recognizing this particular issue, the VRS made the decision, based on all of their other manning and professional educational shortfalls, that they were going to put the bulk of their professional JNA-trained officers at these higher levels of command, and consequently assume a risk at the lower levels of command which would be filled by individuals who were often reservists and who had nowhere near the professional training and background. So, yeah, I agree. And in fact they recognised that risk and reacted accordingly to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so we understand, with regard to military doctrine at the lower levels, we're talking about such things, are we not, as, for example, the number of kilometres that a unit of a particular size or character should be able to cover?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those things -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As an example.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those things are covered in the combat regulations. But maybe as a better example of that, when you look at a brigade structure, there would be the effort to seed that key command group with professionally trained JNA officers in a commander and Chief of Staff and maybe the operations officer roles. Many of the subordinate commanders who were not required to operate in such a sophisticated manner would be reserve officers who would not have that expertise. So it was at the higher levels of command is where they kind of tried to create that nucleus of professional officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since you mentioned brigade, perhaps just for a moment we can move to the side, and could you give us just a rough understanding of the structure of the VRS in terms of brigades and corps, how that broke itself down.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just kind of general, how is an army put together?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, using the VRS, in April, when they organised, and through May and June, the VRS initially consisted of the Main Staff which was the command and control nucleus of the entire army. Under it, it had initially five combat corps formations. A corps, in the VRS vernacular, probably had between 25 and maybe 50.000, I think in one case even higher than that, number of soldiers assigned, and those people would be broken down into various subordinate components that were referred to as brigades. Each brigade had between 3 and 5.000 soldiers. There would be between some cases five, some cases seven brigades assigned to a corps. Within each brigade, you would have a number of battalions, each between, roughly, 500 or 700 people. You would have three, five, sometimes up to six or seven battalions in a brigade, depending on how it was organised, and then it keeps going lower. In each battalion you would have five or six companies of roughly 100 people. So, I mean, that was how the hierarchy was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the formation of the VRS, one of the difficulties that the VRS experienced with regard to the issue of military doctrine was that it was an underpopulated army; correct? If you follow -- I think you follow what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't necessarily an issue of the military doctrine. What it was, was the fact that they did not have the requisite manpower to accomplish the doctrine. The units themselves were chronically under-manned because the war was not popular, desertion was a fairly regular occurrence. And perhaps more importantly, the leadership of those units were not properly manned either. Either having officers in command positions at those lower levels who are not qualified, or the fact that -- and, again, well known within the VRS, that a lot of the officers who were of Bosnian Serb origin who were in the JNA did not serve in the VRS for a variety of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. One of the things that I'm driving at here, and perhaps I used the incorrect language, is that in terms of one of the fundamental principles that guides military doctrine with regard to the issue of the population of an army is that there is a recognition of a ratio that should exist between attacking forces and defending forces. I think it is a three to one ratio, is one of the fundamental principles that come out, and it has come out through the ages of warfare. And that is what I was driving at with regard to the issue of the army being an underpopulated army, among other things.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't look at it those terms. I look at it in terms of when one looks at the establishment of the army, their basic structure and what their -- in my army we call it the table of organisation and equipment, and it reflects the manning, that the units were chronically undermanned for the size of the units and the type of units that they had. Now your application of three to one at a particular point of attack, you know, during the course of combat operations as one saw from 1992 to 1995, they would be able to generate the requisite ratios that they needed by moving units in from other areas of the country, or in other areas they would be able to compensate by using fires or other forms of combat power. So I don't look at it in the same view that you do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And since you have introduced a new a concept here which is the concept of fires, perhaps can you explain to the Chamber what fires -- what the that means when you use that particular term.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. When I use the term "fires," I am referring to artillery, mortars, things of that nature. It is considered to be a combat multiplier rather than when one looks at how a military may attack and how a military will generate combat power at the point of attack or at a point on the battlefield where it wants to, troops, the manoeuvre formations, fires, the artillery units, those are all part of that equation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the Bosnian Muslim army, would it be fair to say that you do not have any exact figure for what the population was of that army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. But I am aware that the population of the Bosnian Muslim army did well exceed that of the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the leadership of the Bosnian Muslim army, those individuals, some of the individuals we were speaking about yesterday, Mr. Rasim Delic, Mr. Halilovic, Mr. Hadzihasanovic, among others, all had previously been in the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that this was a unique situation because what had happened was the country had fallen into a civil war. What you had here was you had all participants in the conflict working under some of the same, if not -- well, I put it that way, some of the same historical understanding of how to wage a war. They all were inculcated with the notion of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, they were all trained the same way, so, as a result, their views on how to conduct military operations all tended to be very familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the issue concerning the amalgamation of the various aspects of the VRS, was the VRS also comprised of an independent police unit, or were those individuals who were actually part of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with what independent police unit you might be referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm asking a question. I'm asking the question whether there was an independent police units that you came across.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an independent protection regiment, the 65th Protection Regiment that worked for the Main Staff, but within the structure of the VRS there were no independent units. If you are referring to the special police brigade that operated not with the -- that wasn't under the army's control nominally; that was under the Ministry of Interior. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You -- yes. And the 66th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the 65th protection regiment that worked for the Main Staff, what did you understand their responsibilities to be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buy the former doctrine --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. They were supposed to be in charge of protecting key facilities and things of that nature. They basically worked for the Military District command, and they were in charge of the security of many of the key military logistical or other facilities. During the actual conflict, the 65th Protection Regiment was used as an assault force and would frequently be found all over the battlefield engaged in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you indicated they were under the Ministry of Interior. And was there --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The special police brigade was under the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 65th Protection Regiment was directly under the command of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Ah, okay. Good. Now, with regard to the Drina Corps, the Drina Corps was not, shall we say, a child of the JNA, was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. The corps headquarters had no former JNA lineage as the other corps did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when -- and when was the Drina Corps formed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the date that it was organised, at least the headquarters was organised, is the 1st of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the Drina Corps when you said that they had no JNA lineage, I take it that by that you mean they -- it was a hodgepodge put together, as opposed to the other corps that had some form of structure that had been pre-existing before the JNA left?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it "hodgepodge," but certainly it did not have the benefit of the nucleus of a former JNA Corps to build around, like, for example, the East Bosnia corps which was made of the nucleus of the former JNA 17th Corps or the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps headquarters which was made up of the nucleus of the former JNA 4th Corps. So that that respect when they created the Drina Corps headquarters, it required them to pull resources from other elements in order to create that. They did not have that JNA nucleus to build around from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where did these elements come from, given the fact that all other soldiers would have belonged to other units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- in this regard, the soldiers themselves, the brigades were relocated from one corps, the older, either East Bosnia Corps or Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which shared responsibility for Eastern Bosnia. So the actual brigade elements themselves were just resubordinated. The personnel that made up the corps headquarters came from either the Main Staff, the corps commander, for example, the 1st Corps commander, General Zivanovic, before he was the corps commander in the Drina Corps, he was the chief of artillery for the Main Staff. Other officers would come in from other locations in the army, so they just drew them from those locations. But the units that ultimately made up the Drina Corps existed in -- as units in other forms and were just simply resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of command and control, could you give the Chamber is rough understanding of what is meant by those terms.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a military sense, command and control is the process by which the individual who is in charge is able to issue orders. Those orders flow down to the subordinates who would follow them, and that the subordinates' compliance with those orders flows back up to the individual who issued them. Very simply put, and, of course, within the context -- you know, much of what we call military doctrine revolves around the processes that take place within that to ensure that those people give orders, that they're transmitted down to subordinates, that they're complied, and the compliance of those orders is again transmitted back up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the JNA and the Territorial Defence, I suggest to you that this is an area where doctrines would diverge? And, if I might, because I see -- I see your mind is turning ahead. Let me make the following proposition to you, which you then can accept or reject, or discuss with me. Which is: the JNA command and control system consisted of unit commands, institution directorates, specialized administrative and command structure. The TDF consisted of territorial staffs, territorial unit commands, territorial institution directorates, and specialized administrative and command organs dealing with specific spheres in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I see where you're driving now. Certainly the JNA command system was organised along more traditional lines, and the Territorial Defences command and control system was organised on a much more decentralised level to reflect the fact that in an occupied country, the command and control system that the JNA had in place would not be able to exist, just because obviously the JNA would not be able to exist like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the distinction between these two doctrines as they relate to command and control, they would directly affect, would they not, issues concerning subordination and discipline?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree that they would affect issues dealing with subordination. Potentially they would deal with issues related to discipline. I -- again, I don't know many of the issues related to the Territorial Defence because relative, particularly to where my field of expertise is with respect to the Drina Corps in July 1995, it was operating off of the JNA command and control model, not that of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue you have just raised, which is that it was operating off of the JNA model, I'd like a little help here, if I could with regard to what I understand to be in command and control areas, that they're basically two kind of command and control principles. One is, as we have been discussing, the decentralised fashion, and one is what we have left a little bit more open which is the centralised form of command and control. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the VRS, is it your contention that they were a centralised form of command and control with a subordinate staff population that was - and I may be being a bit bold in my position - but in large measure, populated by officers and reservists who had not received that kind of training and had come from the military doctrine of Territorial Defence, that being a decentralised form of command and control.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I think -- it's inaccurate, because while you had different models that the Territorial Defence and the JNA operated under with respect to how they would be expected to perform in wartime, the reality was that the officers were one and the same. The active officers, I mean, even the reserve officers, they were not trained differently; they all received the same training. And, you know, again one of the reasons for me, why we never focussed on the Territorial Defence model is that in April of 1992, I'm sorry, in June of 1992, I believe it is, the Republika Srpska creates their Law on Army and the Law on Defence, which lays out exactly what the command and control apparatus of the army will be. So that is the model that they followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you that -- that the reality of what was occurring on the ground and the reality of what is written in the book brings to mind there's many a slip twixt the cup and the lip, and that the model that was written was not the model that was in fact followed?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Guy-Smith kindly speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could Mr. Guy-Smith identify the time-period he is talking because the question is extremely general.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Not a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period of time that you were focussed on, which is 1995, July.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, as I guess you would take from the thrust of my reports, and on command with respect to the Main Staff corps and brigade and the narratives, I would disagree with that assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I would assume that you would. I want to move to an issue where I'm sure we probably will agree.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith is inaudible, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to move to an issue which I'm sure you and I will agree upon which is the importance of the unity of command.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir, that is an important principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Chamber what unity of command means.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hopefully I will paraphrase it correctly from the relevant Law on the Army where it is discussed. But unity of command is the principle that there is one commander, that the orders from that commander are to be followed, that outside influences should not penetrate that relationship. It's basically, it's singular command. And in the case of the VRS ultimately, singular command of the army under the Supreme Commander, which would be President Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going add to a component to that and see if you agree. I think it is something that you may have previously said which is that you cannot have a function where you have multiple commanders in one unit.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think even if one looks back at the trials of the Soviet army facing the German invasion where they had multiple commanders and one saw the results I think everybody learned a lessen that that doesn't work. You have to have a singular commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the singular commander, I believe you mentioned for Republika Srpska was Radovan Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of position of the President, he was in fact the commander of chief of the armed forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And directly under him with regard to matters military would have been General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With matters with respect to the VRS, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would that be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it suits you, you have two more minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was saying for the record I would like to mention something that I forgot to mention at the beginning of the session this morning, that we are still sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I just -- I forgot something. If I could have the 65 ter number which is 6292 admitted as defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted. And may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could please have Exhibit P2248 up on the screen, and I'm going specifically be going to page 4, section 2 of that particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of unity of command --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, if I could maybe conveniently stop you here. Both versions I'm looking at are in Serbo-Croatian, so -- I am assuming one version should be an English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, you can read Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler has the documents in front of him, perhaps he can refer to the -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we go. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- set of documents in hard copy -- [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. If you prefer to use your hard copy.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that I know what we're talking about, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But if you want to go to your hard copy, please do so. Whatever works best for you. It works best for me in hard copy because I'm going blind.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just works best for me in a language I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. With regard to the issue of unity of command, you discuss in your report the 1984 JNA brigade rules, I'm starting at section 2.0, with regards to the responsibilities of a brigade commander. And understanding that this is dealing with the issue of command of a brigade, you state: "The command of the brigade is part of an integrated system of command and control which are based on adopted principles of command?" And I believe we have, for the most part, already discussed those issues, have we not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, they were the adopted principles of command that were articulated by the JNA and SFRY armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent. I'm not going to concern myself with the second sentence, but with regard to the third sentence, it says: "To this end command must integrated, continuous, secure, flexible, effective, and operational?" And you go on to say, once again quoting from a previous JNA manual, which is a 1983 JNA manual for the work of command and staffs: "The command relationship is based on the principle of unity, unity of command and subordination. It is defined in the relationship between the superior and his subordinate. The command relationship pervades the entire system of the armed forces from the SFRY Presidency to the soldiers." I'd like to stop there for a moment. Because of what you have told us here, I take it that when we were discussing earlier the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic, and his direct subordinate, Ratko Mladic, that this is the exact principle that was adopted by the RS that had pre-existed at the time of the JNA. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is a fair characterization.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to continue here. "It is an obligation to execute the tasks set by one's superior or competent officers and organs in an accurate and proper manner." And before we go any further, you have -- there are two different concepts there. One is superior, and the other is competent officer. Do you interpret the term here "competent officer" to involve an understanding of a hierarchical relationship, or does it have to do the ability of the officer to do something?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attribute this within the hierarchical nature in so much as the competent officer is one who is appointed to do a certain -- appointed within the hierarchy to be able to give those types of orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And you continue, so we'll continue: "And act in accordance with the military regulations in their execution." And I take by that you're not only referring to the general military regulations that were promulgated at the time but also orders that would occur at the time of battle, for example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go to the next sentence which is: "Any disruption in the command relationship, such as circumvention of or wrongful interference with the chain of command is a sign of military disorganisation." Now I take it that sentence embodies the concept that we were referring to before when you were talking about the failed experiments with multiple, I believe, you said Russians fighting against the Nazis in World War II?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in this particular context where it is referring to is more along the lines of a situation where other officers would come in, or even non-military officers, political officials would come in and try and give orders or try and influence the chain of command in a particular military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I see. With regard to what you've just said, in terms of the issues as they relate to military doctrine, being the mechanism whereby the national objectives are engaged, if you have distinct national objectives, would it, in your estimation, be fair to say that the attempt to influence one national objective to another would be something that would be of concern with regard to the language that is here, in terms of wrongful interference? And that was probably in-artfully put.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I don't understand what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me do that again for you. With regard to the issue of the unity of command, the unity of command necessarily flows from military doctrine; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And the military doctrine necessarily flows from the national objective that exists at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Where you have distinct national objectives; for example, the difference between what was occurring in FRY during, let's say, 1994, the embargo time, and the Republika Srpska, the attempt to influence would be an example of the wrongful interference that we are discussing here. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess where I would have difficulty in answering that question is only in so much as I don't know what the national objectives of the FRY were in that respect. It wasn't an area of particular study for me. So I can't particularly --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- help out on that question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at it, then, not in the specific abstract but the general abstract, if you have competing national objectives, would the attempt to influence be something that would be of concern with regard to the language that is contained herein?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- you're too abstract now. I just don't track what you're trying to ask, sir. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you talking, Mr. Guy-Smith, are you talking about completing national objectives within the same nation or in two different nations?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm actually talking about competing national objectives within two different nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then -- and I guess this is it why the witness can't follow you. I can't follow you too. Because -- because, sir, within the particular nation, either of the two, each one has its own objective, and there is nothing competing with that. If you have a competing objective with another nation, that's what brings you to war with that nation.
