utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. I mean, this is a summary that I -- and I summarized for my conclusion whenever there is any doubt, and one of the reasons why I so heavily footnote my document - and, in fact, on the electronic version you can actually pull up the document in question that has been footnoted - I always revert back to -- you know, the reader back to the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I believe with regard to the quoted language "security operations," we've discussed that. And the other one was the quoted language here, "let the prisoners go," was that another place where there was a technical error with regard to the information that's contained within the report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. I believe the exact translation is "let them go," if I'm correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to these issues -- and the only reason I'm asking the question is because when we started your testimony you were kind enough to correct a discrete portion of your report by deleting some language in a footnote so that your report would be technically accurate.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But I'm operating under the assumption that everybody has my prior transcripts and all the prior corrections that have been made over the course of trials on this, and that the corrections that I made was one that had not been caught previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. So apart from what I have just noted, then, any other corrections to be made to your report are, as you put it, to be found in your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe there were a couple of identified footnote citations and things of that nature that were either transposed or in the wrong location, and I think we have dealt with them as part of my prior testimony, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your testimony here, however, we have not had the benefit of those corrections; correct? I don't mean here today; I mean just since the time you have been with us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, like I said, they're all former transcripts. I don't know what has gone by with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You just -- you don't by any chance know off the top of your head --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just make sure you are near the mike, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You don't know by any chance off the top of your head just how many days you have testified in these prior proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Um, I'm thinking about 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm thinking you're about right. Okay. You mentioned to us in your testimony that the -- the column size was somewhere between, I believe, 12 and 15.000.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Those are the generally accepted numbers, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And in your narrative, I believe you mentioned that the column size is between 10 and 15.000.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. And I understand that there may be a mere 2.000 in terms of distinction between the two, but is -- are we to rely on the 10 to 15.000 figure or the 12 to 15.000 figure with regard to column size?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir nobody was standing at the beginning of the column with a counter, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right, I appreciate that. But since you are the person who has given both of those numbers, I'm just trying to figure out which number we should rely upon with regard to the column size?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm comfortable with the 12 to 15.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. When Pandurevic, on the 15th of -- I believe it was the 16th, I'm sorry, July, decided to let the column through, this was in reaction, as I understood it, to his appreciation which had been developing the day before, of the magnitude of the military threat that the column posed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the military threat that the column posed, I believe you've told us that it's estimated that one-third of the column was armed.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that, I believe that in some of the footage some of the last footage that we saw yesterday, we saw at least one or two soldiers -- I'm sorry, one or two individuals in camouflage clothing, I believe, carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the decision that was made to let the column through, that decision, would you characterize that as being an independent decision, a decision that comes from a centralised command structure, or a decision that comes from a decentralised command structure?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that would apply. I mean, the decision was made by Colonel Pandurevic, the lawfully appointed commander after that brigade. Colonel Pandurevic made the decision on his own and then notified his superior command that he had done that. Obviously his superior command did not view that as a decision that they wanted happen. They -- they viewed that as something counter to the orders. But having said that, I don't think that that particular decision is characterized either as -- under a centralised or a decentralised structure. It happened within the structure of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You raise an interesting point because you say that -- that his superior command did not view that as a decision they wanted to happen; they viewed that as something counter to the orders. So with regard with that decision having been made counter to the orders, I'm trying to get some understanding here with regard to how such a decision by Pandurevic falls into the discussion that we've been having in a more general sense, admittedly, concerning command and control. Because it seems to me what you just said is that he didn't follow orders.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. He didn't follow orders of his superior command, which were to essentially engage in and destroy the column to the extent that he could. The orders that he gave as the brigade commander, he was entitled to give as the commander. So, I mean, again, I don't know how that particular discussion falls under a centralised or a decentralised structure. He was operating within the centralised structure of the army of the Republika Srpska. He gave an order that he was entitled to give as the commander, even though it ran counter to the guidance he had received from his superior organs. And then he informed them of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. You said guidance which is distinct to an order. Is it your testimony that he received a guidance with regard to how this should be handled or he received an order with regard to the issue of this particular column?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is his orders were to engage the column. So I don't want to make it sound like he had -- there was an option, an optional thing. He was sent back from Zepa with various re-enforcements in order to defend his zone and engage the column, and that is what they expected him to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it correct that before he gave this order he had sent a report to them telling them of the problems he was faced with and asking for assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If going back in time, when he arrives on 15 July, he does report back to the superior command, as well as subsequently informing them of the -- his growing perception of the strength of the column and everything else. By the 16th of July, he makes the judgement, as the man on the ground there, that he can't successfully engage the column and that the best thing that he can do is to allow it to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. Prior to the 16th, he had reported the problems that he was faced with and asked for assistance from his superiors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And in fact prior to 16th he was heavily involved in combatting the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did he get that assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I think he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He did get assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Through the day of the 15th as well as the 16th, additional reinforcements were being rushed to the Zvornik battlefield area, so he was receiving reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But still allowed the column to go through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he -- again, as the commander on the ground, he made that decision in order to allow the column to pass --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it because notwithstanding the re-enforcements, the column was still overwhelming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, that is a point of contention in the ongoing trial. It is my position, based on my reading from the documents that that is it in fact correct. He made the judgement that even with the reinforcements that were coming in, that he could not militarily contest the passage of the column without taking a significant number of casualties. His position is that he allowed the column to pass as a humanitarian gesture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of any disciplining that would have been done in relation to his decision to let the column pass, who would have been his superior to make such a determination of discipline?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His first level superior to make that decision would have been the corps commander, Colonel Radislav Krstic. Above that, would have been General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And above Mladic, would there have been Karadzic, or would it have stopped, in your estimation, based upon the laws that you have analysed and reviewed, and your understanding of the history of this discrete period of time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe that given the laws that I reviewed, that certainly as the Supreme Commander and also you know the minister of Defence, there would have been a political component as well, and certainly Karadzic and the minister of Defence would have had a say in it as well. And when I talk about discipline it's not just if the context of a military court martial, so to speak. It could also be a decision to relieve him of his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What other thing -- I understand the issue with court martial. But apart from relieving him from his command, what other kinds of discipline were available to be imposed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it depends on what context. If we're talking about a disciplinary context of his failure to follow orders, it would have been -- you know, he would have been potentially or could have been potentially relieved of command and reassigned. It could have been administratively demoted or sanctioned in another way. If we're talking about the context of his involvement in the criminal acts related to his decisions and those of the Zvornik Brigade certainly the military court system would have been a process that should have been played.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Thank you. I'm going to move away from that issue and go to something which is perhaps more concrete because we don't yet have an understanding of -- of geographically the Srebrenica enclave. And I'm hoping you can be of some assistance us in that regard. I don't know if you still have the --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- the map.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. Yes, sir, I do; it was folded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is P2400. You indicated yesterday that the area that is encircled in purple, as I understood it, represents the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And within the -- within that enclave, there are a number of different cities or settlements; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I've heard the term "Bandera triangle," B-a-n-d-e-r-a. Is the Bandera triangle a specific part of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is geographically an area that is to the south and west of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could scroll -- I'm going to scroll down on the screen. Excellent. Okay. It's an area which is -- and perhaps with the help of the usher here ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you give us a -- an imagistic representation with the use of the trusty electronic pen of the Bandera triangle.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is it the approximate area we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And the Bandera triangle contains within a part of the Jadar river; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the entire -- the entire area, the entire area of the Srebrenica enclave -- that's fine, thank, you Mr. Registrar. You know what, we should probably -- I'm not quite done, if you could mark that -- inside of that triangle with a B to represent Bandera. Could you do that? Do you have a pen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you were referring to the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't think he can mark for you. Somehow I don't think the Judges would like that too much. It is bad enough when either Mr. Harmon or I testify, when I get too far astray here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have that admitted as defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll do this just now. But just before we do that, I don't whether you are able to help us, I see this map is very scant on the legend. Are you able to tell us what the dots on the perimeter of the Srebrenica enclave marked with letters of the alphabet denote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do they denote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are the locations of United Nations outposts that were along the perimeter. They had these observation posts. They were identified alphabetically, and that is what dots depict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D111.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the area that is contained within the -- the purple outline, it's my understanding that area is approximately 60 square kilometres; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your word for that. It sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I actually think I gleaned that from one of your testimonies, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a while, sir. But as I said, I think it sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the left-hand side of the map, up where it says Tuzla, there's an area which is in pink. Do you see that area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if you could scroll down. Scroll down, sorry -- I mean scroll up. Up, down. Okay, stop right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you see where it says BiH?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then it says Tuzla, and there's an area which is in pink?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that depicts the city environs of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is where the city environs of Tuzla, is that also where the airport was located?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the airport is actually located outside and a little to the south of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm done with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, on 16th of April, 1993, Srebrenica was declared a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it never became a demilitarised zone and that there was a standing army within the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in 1995, at the time of the spring, there were a number of different locations throughout the region, specifically I'm referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, where an offensive was mounted by the Bosnian Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this time, this point in time, is probably the most dramatic point in time where there is a breakdown between the Bosnian government and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you would be correct or not. I didn't study the relationship between the -- I assume when you're talking Bosnian, Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I made a mistake I asked you not to make. Precisely so. Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. That was not something that I engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you study at all in your analysis the concerns that the Bosnian Muslim army had with regard to the difficulties that UNPROFOR was creating for its successful winning of the war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- my knowledge of that is, in large part, based on -- and I think it's footnote 72 of my report, the 1999 United Nations report dealing with Srebrenica, and particularly the eastern safe areas that they published, and I believe in that particular report, there is a fair amount of discussion on that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it you would also agree with me that the 28th Division of the Bosnian Muslim army was -- had successfully been tying up a -- two brigades of men from the Drina Corps after the spring offensive and prior to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expand it even more so. I would say that they were successfully tying up at least two brigades of the Drina Corps from the creation of the safe area in 1993 to that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Following up from your last answer, would you agree that the Bosnian Muslim army, in its condition having successfully tied up a number of the Drina Corps brigades, was composed of officers and soldiers who came from the same military doctrine that we have been discussing, promulgated by the JNA from the same laws that we have been discussing in the general sense, and obviously I think you've already told us were JNA officers, as the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the manpower of that particular army, the officers were, to the degree that they were former JNA officers, or trained by the JNA, and the manpower, again, all did their mandatory conscripted service within the JNA except for those, of course, the younger kids joining the army who began their military service you know after the JNA had already gone away. So to that degree, I think that's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And, I mean, obviously because we're dealing with a relatively unique situation that being of a civil war, in which a standing army, that being the JNA, ultimately had a breakup in which officers that had previously all been together went into separate armies and oftentimes armies against each other, it makes sense, having come from much of the same tradition, whether they be as we've just discussed, Bosnian Muslims, or Bosnian Serbs, or Croatians, that they would follow that which they had learned over many years as professional soldiers.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in the earlier years of the war. Gradually as they learn their own lessons and develop perhaps unique tactics or unique operational lessons from their own combat experience, they might differ. But by and large everyone followed along the lines of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I think that you even make such a comment in what is at 2248 at paragraph 1. -- 1.4 where you indicate: "However for a variety of reasons, few updated regulations were published by the VRS during the war." And your footnote is: "Given the linkage of the between the Officer Cadre of the VRS and the VJ, it is not surprising there was almost no migration away from established JNA (and later) VJ military regulatory basis." And then you have one notable exception was the publication of the provisional regulations on service in the army of the Serbian republic, issued on 18 August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir, for the VRS, that is exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What -- one final question with regard to something that you have mentioned in your report, the same report, at P2248, and that's with regard to -- you mention an organisation known as the 30th Personnel Centre. Did you have occasion to study in your analysis the 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the in-depth mechanics of the centre per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge of the centre reflects the fact that the former professional officers of the JNA who were assigned to the VRS were still administratively dealt with the by the VJ 30th Personnel Centre. That's the degree that I am aware of it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And you can take it no further than that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. Helicopters. Are you aware of the -- I'm going start with the findings that were made in the Krstic Judgement, with regard to the issue of helicopters. And by that I'm referring to paragraph 24 in which the Trial Chamber heard credible and largely uncontested evidence of a consistent refusal by the Bosnian Muslims to abide by the agreement to demilitarise the safe area. "The Bosnian Muslim helicopters flew in violation of the no-fly zone. The ABiH opened fire towards Bosnian Serb lines and moved through the safe area. The 28th Division was continually arming itself, and at least some humanitarian aid coming into the enclave was appropriated by the ABiH." The reason I'm asking if you are familiar that, is you told us that you had worked on the appeal of Krstic, and I take it that you may have well read the judgement. It goes on to say: "To the Bosnian Serbs it appeared that Bosnian Muslim forces in Srebrenica were using the 'safe area,'" which is in quotes, "as a convenient base from which to launch offensives against the VRS and that UNPROFOR was failing to take any action to prevent it. General Halilovic admitted that Bosnian Muslim helicopters had flown in violation of the no-fly zone, and he had personally dispatched eight helicopters with ammunition for the 28th Division. In moral terms, he did not see it as a violation of the safe area agreement, given that the Bosnian Muslims were so poorly armed to begin with." So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just clarity on the question, Your Honour. Is the question whether Mr. Butler is aware of that passage that Mr. Guy-Smith has read from the Krstic Judgement? That the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're waiting for that question, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read the Judgement. I can't say that that particular -- or at least parts of that come to mind. I am aware of General Halilovic's comments. Going perhaps back to the beginning where I base my knowledge of that particular issue, and again, referring to footnote 72 of my revised narrative, which is the United Nations report on Srebrenica, after our exchange I wanted to be sure that I was in fact correct, and I would refer the reader back to paragraph 222 of the United Nations report where they in fact acknowledge their knowledge of these helicopter flights into the eastern safe areas, and in May of 1995, the fact that one had been shot down. So that's where I'm basing as an initial point of departure, from my knowledge. I'm also aware obviously of VRS documents which date their knowledge of these helicopter flights occurring as well as their efforts to interdict it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In addition to that, are you aware of the testimony of General Hadzihasanovic of the 6th of April, 2005, with regard to this issue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You've mentioned that your awareness of Halilovic's testimony in this regard, although did you not rely upon it, as I understand, are you aware of the fact that there was testimony also received with regard to the specific issue, by that I'm just referring to the issue of helicopter flights and the violation of the no-fly zone by the Bosnian Muslim army from Mr. Radinovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of -- I guess it was profess or Radinovic's testimony. I don't know whether he specifically -- he was over a period of a number of days too. I don't recall at this juncture whether or not he stated that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of the testimony of any members of UNPROFOR or DutchBat with regard to that particular issue? Once again, the issue of the flying of helicopters.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't recall the testimony, whether that issue came up or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And finally, I'd like to show you a document -- or I believe that we have agreement with regard to a document. And I'm looking across the -- across the landscape to my colleague on the other side, which is the document that had been previously discussed with Mr. Williams, which is 1D01-1881. You have a different number because you have a number from a different case. But it's the same document. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the document, the final analysis of the Srebrenica and Zepa air lift [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... that's correct. And it's dated the 17th of February, 1996, and I believe there is an agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... You were right. I agree with Mr. Guy-Smith. We agreed that that this document should come into evidence to clarify the matter of the helicopters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: See, the helicopter discussion wasn't so bad after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think we should give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have an exhibit number on that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. That's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D112.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if I could have but one brief moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I made you a promise at the beginning of my examination of you, and I hope I kept my promise, and I haven't kept you for too long. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon. Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one or two questions I would like to put to you. I would like to clarify a few points in your report. First of all, since you analysed all the military operations around Srebrenica, in mid-July, did you see any documents stating that there were VJ military in that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my first question. Furthermore, on looking at the map of this area, we see that the Drina delineates the border in that area. The border between Bosnia and the former republican -- Yugoslav republic. And the former Yugoslav republic, in the north of the area. So this is my question. On the other side of the river was there the Serb army? Was the Serb army on the other side of the river? And could they see what was happening close by?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what you mean by could they see what's happening. As opposed to -- you know, did they have the means to know what was happening? And the reason why I qualify that is, is obviously if you're talking about sight lines across the Drina river, they're very limited. But some of the activity, for example, in one particular instance one of the survivors of an execution notes that the bus convoy that was taking him from the Bratunac area to the area in Zvornik, actually at one point crossed over one of the bridges into Serbian territory, drove up and then re-crossed back over at Zvornik. There are other instances where individuals who attempted to escape, actually swam or came across the Drina river or found other ways across the river into Serbia and were apprehended mostly by the local police forces there, and then those forces in contact with the Republika Srpska military made arrangements to turn them back over again to RS custody, with respect to Srebrenica. So given the types of activity that was occurring, again situation-dependant on which particular unit you're talking about and where they are, you know, there were opportunities for them to know. If you're limiting it to just mere sight line, it might be pretty difficult in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your rather accurate answer. I have another question for you. This is something you discussed in your report, and we have discussed it quite extensively. Personnel from the Ministry of Interior, policemen. And this is not very clearly explained in your report. I'm not quite sure whether these people belonged to the military police or to the civilian police. I believe that they -- the military police was present on the ground, and I believe that the civilian police was also there, and what I'm talking about is the Zvornik area. Now, as far as the civilian police is concerned, in this particular case, was it placed under the command or the order of the MUP, or was it placed under the command of the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the police that are operating in the Zvornik municipality from roughly the 15th and beyond, they remained under the command of the head of the CSB, Mr. Vasic. However, they were operating under the control of the army. They were actually sweeping various areas of the battlefield, where they were engaged in either being engaged against the column as well as securing some of the rear areas and they were doing that under the control of the military commander, Colonel Pandurevic. When the RS police forces from, for example, the 2nd Sekovici Detachment and the 1st P JP which moved from the road area on the morning of the 15th and then moved to the Zvornik area as part of reinforcing Colonel Pandurevic for his fight against the column, again, they still remained under the command of Colonel Borovcanin. They operated under the control of the Colonel Pandurevic, and that command relationship, as it were, is codified under Republika Srpska law in the Ministry of the Interior. And it notes that when these various police units are operating in a military zone and operating in concert with the army, that while the army commander has some ability -- while the police commander remains in command of the unit, they operate under the direction of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your report, and this is something I heard from Mr. Vasic, at one point in time he refused to cooperate with the military when it came to mass executions, for instance. That's what he says anyway.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, going back to the Republika Srpska Law on the Ministry of the Interior, one of the aspects of that law is that before the police forces fall under military control, that the minister of defence and the minister of the interior jointly agree as to what the limits of those tasks will be. And obviously both the army and the police commanders are aware of what those limits are. So as long as the military commanders are giving orders within the limits of that defined resubordination, if you will, the police have to follow them. If the military commander is giving orders outside the limits of that prearranged agreement, then the police are not obligated to follow them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Now to follow up on this, I -- we also discussed Military Tribunals, and we discussed the fact that the military, like Colonel Pandurevic, could be court martialed because he had not obeyed the orders. I have another question in this regard. Was one single military, who was prosecuted for the crimes that were committed in Srebrenica? And when I say prosecuted, I mean prosecuted by the Military Tribunals in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one, according to what you know, not a single one has been prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one last question. You discussed at length General Zivanovic's replacement by General Krstic on the 13th of July. I don't know if you know about this, because in your report you say that the reasons for his replacement were not very clear. Have you since had any documents that would shed some light on the reasons for which he got replaced? And how important is it that he got replaced?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, at the time, particularly as these reports were drafted, didn't know the answer to that. As the investigation has continued, there were two general stories related to General Zivanovic being replaced. One particular story is that he was replaced as a result of his health reasons and, of course, General Zivanovic notes that when he was interviewed by the ICTY. There's actually a very quick clip where General Zivanovic is talking about his blood pressure being something over like over 200 over 300 at this point. So, I mean, his story is in fact that, you know, he ultimately was relieved and retired as a result of his health. There is another story floating around obviously, and again difficult to corroborate, that he was identified using military resources from the Drina Corps and from the 5th Engineers for his own personal gain, and -- respect the construction of a chicken farm in some location. General Mladic was very strict about those particular types of issues. And the other story going around is that General Zivanovic was in fact, you know, replaced because of his use of that, those military resources for non-military issues. I don't know that it -- that's particularly important to the larger Srebrenica crime base, where it was important for us is because as a component of General Krstic's proceedings, he hotly contested when he assumed command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It was very clear in the trial against General Krstic. It was important to know, of course, when he had actually assumed the command of the army. But in this case, this might be somewhat less important. That was my last question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I wasn't going to ask any questions, but I just want it ask -- get an answer to part of Judge Picard's questions that she put to you and part of which was not answered. At page 68, lines 11 to 12, she asked you whether -- I beg your pardon. Lines 15 to 16. Line 16 specifically: Was there Serb army on the other side of the river?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specifically tell you where the VJ military units were located along the Drina river, sir. I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But were they located along the Drina river at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- again, I'm not familiar with the dispositions of where those units would have been in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Any questions Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I do, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge Picard as you some questions, Mr. Butler, about could the army see what was happening from the territory it occupied? In other words, in the FRY, was there a direct line of sight to events that were occurring in the Republika Srpska? Let me take you to the map, P2400, Mr. Butler, and ask you -- first of all, there is an red dot near Kozluk contiguous with the river, the Drina river. Do you see that red dot? In fact the right-hand edge of that dot is on the river. Have you been to the Kozluk site, or do you know about where it was located in respect of the Drina river?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know where it is it located in respect of the Drina river.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where was the mass execution side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was actually right on the river-bank area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And on the river-bank area in the RS; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the other side was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in respect of -- you mentioned in your evidence that some people fled the enclave and swam across the Drina river. They were captured by what units, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which units captured them per se. I know that where the investigation gains visibility of them is that they are turned over to the Serbian police who then coordinate with the VRS units on the other side of the border to turn these people back over to the VRS custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were in fact people -- some of the people who went across the river turned back over to the RS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what -- do you know their fate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe all of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were some people who went across the river and were detained by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia police in whatever formation, did they survive?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For Srebrenica, the individuals for Srebrenica, I don't -- at the state of my knowledge when I left, I don't believe so. For Zepa, I am aware that those that crossed over the river did survive. So I can't say whether or not the investigation has found any -- you know, in the recent years has found any individuals from Srebrenica who made it across the river who were then returned back to their custody and survived. I just don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the answer to the question is you don't know the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I know what my state of knowledge is. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, just a quick transcript correction which would be on page 68, line 10, I believe that, Mr. Butler's answer was, No, ma'am. And at the balance of that line is to Judge Picard's question. So just to make sure that is taken care of. Further cross-examination by Mr. Guy-Smith:

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know with regard to those people who went into FRY, when they were stopped by the police, which police they were stopped by? Were they stopped by the customs police? Were they stopped by the local police? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what the relationship those police had with any part of the government, as to whether or not they were under the auspices under the Ministry of Interior; were they under the auspices of some other organisation, Ministry of Defence? Do you have any information whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, if he doesn't know which police they are, how would he know which department they fell under?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: With regard to the statement that you made, you told us that there were people who crossed over the river who were, as I understand it, not returned to the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Related to those individuals fleeing from the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you tell us the fate of those people from the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding that those individuals who crossed the Drina river from Zepa, that they were in fact, once in Serbia -- first of all, the RS wanted them back, that the Serbian government refused and put them under the protection of the ICRC elements that were in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Picard has one more question to ask. I'm sorry, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's to follow up on these proceedings. Were there people who crossed the river who managed to flee and who were not arrested afterwards by the Serbian police or army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of any individual who came out of that Srebrenica process who crossed the Drina river, managed to either transit through Serbia or whatever state, and then has subsequently approached the Office of the Prosecutor and made that known. So I'm not aware of anyone who fits that criteria, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Only with regard to the last question asked by Her Honour, which is, I don't recall you mentioning any arrest by the Serbian army. Now, you previously mentioned the Serbian police. The question has become somewhat different from where we were initially. Is it your understanding that the arrests that were made were made by the local police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is I don't know who made the arrests or that initial detention. Where we gained visibility on them, from my perspective, is that when they're in the custody of the local police elements and that those police elements are contacting the military counterparts in the VRS, primarily the Zvornik and the Bratunac Brigade, identifying that they have individuals and that they want the VRS to take custody of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- I just want to ask -- I want to see if I can refresh Mr. Butler's recollection on something; it may or may not refresh his recollection. Further re-examination by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, In reviewing intercepts, did you review any intercepts where the Republika Srpska army demanded the return of -- to use the -- I think I will be using, the terms of the intercept, Give me back my Turks. Do you recall an intercept like that? And could you tell us, first of all, if you recall that intercept and what you know about that intercept and its consequences?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do recall the intercept. The intercept is a conversation with -- and Colonel Beara is one of the correspondents. If I'm not mistaken, General Krstic is another one of the correspondents. And they are discussing the fact that they're aware that hundreds of Muslims from the -- you know, former Zepa enclave had been crossing the Drina river and were in Serbia and that they were further aware that the Serbs would not turn those individuals back over to the custody of the Republika Srpska and, of course, the army personnel were not happy with that development.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So that leads me to my next question because I want to just clarify this point. You say in your answer that they were aware that these people were in Serbia. They are further aware that the Serbs would not turn over these individuals, you know, back to the custody of the authorities of the army of the RS. Which brings me to my question. Did the Serbian authorities in that context of that intercept, to your knowledge, turn over the people referred to in the intercept you've described? In other words was Beara, was Krstic successful in getting from the authorities in Serbia a certain number of people they had in their custody?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to Zepa, I believe the answer is no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do not intend on playing ping-pong. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't intend on doing that. I don't have any further questions. And I do have one housekeeping matter that has been brought to my attention by the Registrar. It does not relate to Mr. Butler. So I'm be happy to take of it. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Butler, thank you so much for coming. We know are you a busy person, taking time off to come and testify. This brings us to the end of your testimony. Are you now excused. You may stand down. Please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before I turn to you, Mr. Harmon, let's hear the housekeeping matter from Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have been informed most kindly by the Registrar that I misspoke myself. And I called up the wrong 65 ter number at page 43, line 4. Defence exhibit 108 should be properly 65 ter number 6590, and I think what I did is I transposed the 9 and the 5. SO the proper number is 6590.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's how we got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You misspoke earlier. You said 6950 and corrected yourself later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Harmon, next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no additional witnesses for this week, Your Honour, for the remainder of the day, which I understood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. To what date do we postpone?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm informed there are no witnesses for next week, Your Honour, and I can give you the schedule through the Court legal officer. I don't have it at my disposal, at my fingertips right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- actually the 8th is a public holiday. Is it further postponed to -- no, no, it is not. Shall we postpone to the 8th then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The matter stands adjourned until the 8th of June, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.
